rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the facts and separates the money, driver, and infrastructure lenses cleanly. Its “Rivian adds Tesla-style plugs and opens its network with no automaker partner in sight” is a usable trade angle; B’s “After Tesla... The proprietary-charger era is fading” drags in an outside trend and pretends this update proves it. B also manufactures a markets peg with “Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet,” which is how a decent angle set gets lipstick on its teeth.
gaps_in_A: “whether ‘improves utilization’ is a polite way of saying stalls sit empty” is sharp, but it is still an inference. Keep it as a reporter question until Rivian gives utilization data.
“why no automaker deal was struck” pushes slightly past “no partnership with another automaker announced.” Good question, bad declarative frame if evidence never appears.
gaps_in_B: “After Tesla, Rivian opens its charging network to all EVs. The proprietary-charger era is fading.” The Tesla peg and category trend are not in the update. That is not angle generation; that is importing a story you wish you had.

“Rivian just became a charging-network operator. Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet.” Rivian already operated chargers, and no market repricing evidence was supplied. This is CNBC cosplay without the stock chart.

“Different from the revenue angle... this asks ‘does this change how Rivian should be valued’” is a padded duplicate. It splits one financial story into two envelopes and calls the second one distinct.
“could move the needle” is on the blacklist and also exposes the weakness: B knows the revenue scale is missing but still lets the valuation angle swagger around unsupervised.
